content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 213 of the Constitution of India is titled “Power of Governor to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Legislature”. It forms an integral component of The States (Articles 152–237), located within the “The States” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) If at any time, except when the Legislative Assembly of a State is in session, or where there is a Legislative Council in a State, except when both Houses of the Legislature are in session, the Governor is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require:

Provided that the Governor shall not, without instructions from the President, promulgate any such Ordinance if—

(a) a Bill containing the same provisions would under this Constitution have required the previous sanction of the President for the introduction thereof into the Legislature; or

(b) he would have deemed it necessary to reserve a Bill containing the same provisions for the consideration of the President; or

(c) an Act of the Legislature of the State containing the same provisions would under this Constitution have been invalid unless, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, it had received the assent of the President.

(2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of the Legislature of the State assented to by the Governor, but every such Ordinance—

(a) shall be laid before the Legislative Assembly of the State, or where there is a Legislative Council in the State, before both the Houses, and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of the Legislature, or if before the expiration of that period a resolution disapproving it is passed by the Legislative Assembly and agreed to by the Legislative Council, if any, upon the passing of the resolution or, as the case may be, on the resolution being agreed to by the Council; and

(b) may be withdrawn at any time by the Governor.

Explanation.—Where the Houses of the Legislature of a State having a Legislative Council are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of this clause.

(3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which would not be valid if enacted in an Act of the Legislature of the State assented to by the Governor, it shall be void:

Provided that, for the purposes of the provisions of this Constitution relating to the effect of an Act of the Legislature of a State which is repugnant to an Act of Parliament or an existing law with respect to a matter enumerated in the Concurrent List, an Ordinance promulgated under this article in pursuance of instructions from the President shall be deemed to be an Act of the Legislature of the State which has been reserved for the consideration of the President and assented to by him. 1(4) [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted retrospective effect) and omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 27 . CHAPTER V.—THE HIGH COURTS IN THE STATES

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 213 as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. It regulates executive, legislative, or fundamental citizen interests to maintain the rule of law and constitutional supremacy.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) If at any time, except when the Legislative Assembly of a State is in session, or where there is a Legislative Council in a State, except when both Houses of the Legislature are in session, the Governor is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require:
2. Provided that the Governor shall not, without instructions from the President, promulgate any such Ordinance if—
3. (a) a Bill containing the same provisions would under this Constitution have required the previous sanction of the President for the introduction thereof into the Legislature; or
4. (b) he would have deemed it necessary to reserve a Bill containing the same provisions for the consideration of the President; or
5. (c) an Act of the Legislature of the State containing the same provisions would under this Constitution have been invalid unless, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, it had received the assent of the President.
6. (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of the Legislature of the State assented to by the Governor, but every such Ordinance—

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 213 is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 213 (Power of Governor to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Legislature) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 213 is situated in The States (Articles 152–237), governing the “The States” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) If at any time, except when the Legislative Assembly of a State is in session, or where there is a Legislative Council in a State, except when both Houses of the Legislature are in session, the Governor is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require:
2. Provided that the Governor shall not, without instructions from the President, promulgate any such Ordinance if—
3. (a) a Bill containing the same provisions would under this Constitution have required the previous sanction of the President for the introduction thereof into the Legislature; or
4. (b) he would have deemed it necessary to reserve a Bill containing the same provisions for the consideration of the President; or
5. (c) an Act of the Legislature of the State containing the same provisions would under this Constitution have been invalid unless, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, it had received the assent of the President.
6. (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of the Legislature of the State assented to by the Governor, but every such Ordinance—

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 213:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 213 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 213 of the Constitution of India, titled “Power of Governor to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Legislature”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The States (Articles 152–237), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 213 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) If at any time, except when the Legislative Assembly of a State is in session, or where there is a Legislative Council in a State, except when both Houses of the Legislature are in session, the Governor is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require:
(a) Limb 2: Provided that the Governor shall not, without instructions from the President, promulgate any such Ordinance if—
(a) Limb 3: (a) a Bill containing the same provisions would under this Constitution have required the previous sanction of the President for the introduction thereof into the Legislature; or
(a) Limb 4: (b) he would have deemed it necessary to reserve a Bill containing the same provisions for the consideration of the President; or
(a) Limb 5: (c) an Act of the Legislature of the State containing the same provisions would under this Constitution have been invalid unless, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, it had received the assent of the President.
(a) Limb 6: (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of the Legislature of the State assented to by the Governor, but every such Ordinance—
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 213 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 213 across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 213:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 213;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 213 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 213?
Rule: Under Article 213, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 213 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

enhancement.definition: Article 213 empowers the Governor of a State to promulgate Ordinances during the recess of the State Legislature when circumstances exist rendering it necessary to take immediate action. An Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of the State Legislature, but is an extraordinary, temporary power subject to mandatory legislative laying, automatic expiration six weeks post-reassembly, and strict judicial review against colorable re-promulgation.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The Governor's Ordinance-making power is a contingent legislative power designed for urgent situations, not an alternative parallel track of executive law-making. Subverting the State Legislature through repeated re-promulgation without legislative debate is a fraud on the Constitution and a subversion of democratic governance (D.C. Wadhwa; Krishna Kumar Singh).

essentialIngredients: Recess of Legislature: Can be promulgated only when the State Legislative Assembly (or both Houses in a bicameral legislature) is not in session.

Subjective Satisfaction of Governor: Governor must be satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action (exercised on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers under Article 163).

Co-extensive with Legislative Competence: Can enact only on subjects within the State List (List II) and Concurrent List (List III); cannot enact what the State Legislature is incompetent to enact, nor violate Part III rights.

Prior Presidential Instructions: Under the Proviso to Clause (1), the Governor SHALL NOT promulgate an Ordinance without instructions from the President if: (a) A Bill containing the same provisions would have required Presidential sanction for introduction; (b) The Governor would have deemed it necessary to reserve a Bill containing the same provisions for the President under Article 200; (c) An Act containing the same provisions would have been invalid unless reserved for and assented to by the President (e.g., Article 254(2) repugnancy).

Mandatory Laying and Expiration: Must be laid before the Legislative Assembly (and Council); ceases to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of the Legislature, or earlier if disapproved.
Re-promulgation Bar: Repeatedly re-issuing an expired ordinance without legislative tabling is unconstitutional and void (Krishna Kumar Singh).
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Article 213 mirrors Article 123 at the State level, but incorporates specific federal checks through the Presidential instructions proviso.

### 1. The Proviso: Presidential Instructions Check
Unlike Article 123, Article 213 contains a crucial federal restraint: the Governor cannot bypass the Centre on sensitive topics. If an Ordinance impinges on High Court powers, violates a Central Act on the Concurrent List (Article 254), or requires presidential reservation under Article 200, the Governor MUST obtain prior instructions from the President of India before promulgation.

### 2. The Bihar Ordinance Raj & D.C. Wadhwa (1987)
In the State of Bihar, the Executive created an 'Ordinance Raj' between 1967 and 1981, repeatedly re-promulgating 256 ordinances for up to 14 years without ever introducing them as Bills in the State Legislature. A Constitution Bench headed by Chief Justice P.N. Bhagwati struck down this practice as a **subversion of the democratic process and a fraud on the Constitution**.

### 3. The Definitive Benchmark: Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)
A 7-judge Constitution Bench comprehensively resolved the jurisprudence of Article 213:
1. **Laying is Mandatory:** The requirement to lay the ordinance before the legislature under Article 213(2)(a) is mandatory. An executive that fails to lay an ordinance commits a grave constitutional violation.
2. **Re-promulgation is a Fraud:** Re-promulgating ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution and renders the re-promulgated ordinance void ab initio.
3. **Judicial Review:** The satisfaction of the Governor under Article 213(1) is subject to judicial review. While courts do not substitute their subjective assessment, they examine whether the satisfaction is based on relevant material or tainted by mala fides.
4. **Survival of Consequences:** An expired or disapproved ordinance does not confer permanent, irrevocable rights; rights created under it dissolve unless reversing them is impossible or contrary to public interest.
examples: Concurrent List Ordinance Without Presidential Instruction: A State Governor promulgates an Ordinance amending the Indian Contract Act (Concurrent List) within the State in direct contradiction to a Central Act, without obtaining prior instructions from the President. Under the Proviso to Article 213(1) read with Article 254, the Ordinance is void ab initio for lack of Presidential instructions.

The Re-promulgation Trap: A State Government fails to pass a land acquisition bill during the monsoon session. It promulgates an Ordinance under Article 213. When the winter session convenes, the government prorogues the assembly without tabling the ordinance, and re-promulgates it the next day. Applying Krishna Kumar Singh, the re-promulgation is unconstitutional and a fraud on the Constitution.
distinctions: Article 213 (Governor) vs Article 123 (President): The President has no requirement to seek instructions from any higher authority; the Governor must obtain prior instructions from the President for bills requiring presidential assent under the Proviso to Article 213(1).

Executive Rule-Making vs Ordinance Power: Executive rule-making under statutes (subordinate legislation) is derivative and administrative; Ordinance power under Article 213 is plenary legislative power equivalent to an Act of the State Legislature, though temporary in lifespan.
problemApplication: Issue: A State Government promulgates an Ordinance under Article 213 imposing a new municipal tax. When the State Legislature reassembles, the Government deliberately refrains from tabling the Ordinance before the Assembly because it lacks a majority. The Ordinance expires after six weeks, and the Governor immediately re-promulgates the identical Ordinance. Is the re-promulgated Ordinance valid?

Rule: Under Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), the requirement to lay an Ordinance before the Legislature is a mandatory constitutional duty. Deliberately avoiding legislative scrutiny and re-promulgating the ordinance constitutes a fraud on the Constitution and renders the ordinance void.

Application: The State Government used the ordinance power as a parallel legislative track to circumvent its minority status in the Legislative Assembly. This is a direct subversion of parliamentary democracy.
Counterargument: The State asserts that urgent tax collection necessitated immediate action and that the Governor exercised constitutional discretion under Article 213(1).
Conclusion: The re-promulgated Ordinance is unconstitutional, null, and void for being a fraud on the Constitution.
